May I be permitted to quote in this connection two excerpts from an address by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) to the convention of the Canadian Teachers' Federation on August 13, 1946:
I am convinced that real national unity, national pride and love of country can better prevail when teaching is left to provinces and to local organizations under them, to which this right duly belongs. I fail to understand how the cause of education or the cause of Canada could be promoted by an attempt to reduce the privileges and duties of provinces in this vast sector of our national life.
I quote further:
Far from trying to centralize in Ottawa all the functions of government, we are anxious to render more secure and more complete the autonomy of provinces, of all the provinces.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
But no other aspect of provincial autonomy is more important than provincial autonomy in matters of education. No other service established by the provinces in the interest of their people is more essential to the well-being of these people than education.
Every Canadian and every government should choose as its inspirational motto to encourage both races to develop to the full in their respective faith and language. In order to attain more easily the height of success in the field of material progress, there is no better way than to develop the spiritual wealth of the families which make up the Canadian nation as a whole. In a people which believes in God, material and spiritual values are indivisible.
Mr. Speaker, we must, therefore, be grateful to the federal government for having initiated and applied a policy of social justice with a view to the welfare of the family. It has understood that, if fortune does not smile equally on everybody, everybody without distinction must nevertheless be endowed with the means of attaining a state of comparative comfort. Such is the social function of family allowances, whose benefits will be felt by this and future generations. Let the hon. members think of the number of young men who will thus be enabled to safeguard their health, develop their talent and contribute more to the progress and greatness of our country! It will perhaps be possible, before long, to modify this legislation to some extent, in order that it may prove more adequate and more generous as far as large families are concerned.

The Address-Mr. Marquis
Social justice means the protection of the weak and the unemployable. The King government has shown an interest in the citizen through every stage of the latter's life. Family allowances, old age pensions, unemployment and labour benefits, aid to the blind, all these constitute welfare legislation of which we may well be proud.
There remains however a class of people who have not, as yet, benefited from the government's generosity. I refer to the crippled or the invalid who are unable to earn their own livelihood. Their condition is pitiful. They are forced to resort to begging or to accept misery. It seems to me that free, frank and loyal co-operation between the provincial and federal governments might have brought a solution from which these unfortunate people would have benefited.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I nevertheless hope that our own government will give substantial help to these unfortunate members of our great Canadian familj'.
I would not make bold to claim that the state should assume all the obligations and take care of all the problems of the people. Charity and mutual help must continue to draw closer the ties that bind the members of a family. But nevertheless the state could extend to the outcasts of life the generous benefits it has bestowed on children and1 old people.
Mr. Speaker, if the government must balance its budget, a similar obligation is incumbent on the heads of families. That is a pretty heavy task in these difficult times. Family income, including allowances must ensure food, clothing, housing, hygiene and health expenditures and an education consonant with the aspirations and aptitudes of every one. In the labouring class, salaries have been on the rise for the last few years, but on the other hand the prices of necessities of life have reached a higher level.
It is very difficult for people of the middle class to plan a budget. That will not surprise anyone, because when poverty and starvation threaten part of humanity, we must share our resources in order to alleviate the sufferings of the afflicted and protect them from materialistic slavery. However, some profiteers are *overdoing it in a criminal way. They endanger the life of the depressed and starving peoples of Europe as well as the economic security of their own country.
Since I have been a member of parliament,.
I have heard stirring appeals in favour of free enterprise. According to the conservative members of the opposition, free enterprise was supposed to enrich a hundredfold the citizens of our country, who were not too badly off. We know how certain supporters of free enterprise speculated on feed, feed grains, meat, butter *and other necessities.
We are in favour of private enterprise, but provided it is truly free. It will be free, if the wealthy do not reduce the workers, the farmers or the middle class people to slavery,, if cartels and monopolies do not control production or hoard up goods in order to raise prices unduly. It will be free if the State does not take over all undertakings or properties so as to* transform the common people into mere robots; finally, it will be free if it does not become a slave to economic or political dictatorship.
I do not believe in Toryism, which would give a free hand to monopolies whose hunger for wealth has for a long time been curbed by war controls; nor do I believe in socialism whose aim is not to plan our economy but rather to put it under the domination of the government through the control of every individual's activities.
To my mind, it is the duty of the State to lead the -various classes in the path of order and progress, to ensure a proper balance between ithe different groups of citizens, to protect the weak against the strong, but not to enslave them. Briefly, its duty is to curt>
abuses and not- to wait for them ito vanish through the force of circumstances or the evolution of events, as claimed by members of the Conservative party.
If the farmer could fight on equal terms with certain intermediaries, if the consumer could freely discuss prices with certain distributors of commodities, then we would have a free economy. But as soon as one group enforces its will on another, you have a dictatorship. The Liberal party's policy has been to prevent such dictatorship and I take it upon myself to suggest, in this respect, a: more constant and efficient watchfulness. That is controlled economy, ensuring social justice-to all, and not state socialism, which tends ten rule the citizens' activities in every sphere. Indeed, I believe in a government which leads free citizens and protects them against
The Address-Mr. Marquis

abuses, and not in a Government which monopolizes the public wealth and under which citizens become servants or slaves of the State. In order to protect the weak from the strong, we must not deprive them of their liberty, but give them the means of resisting victoriously.
I believe that at present the best method is to set the prices of essential commodities at a family budget level. Would: it not be advisable to adopt a legislation tending to establish a reasonable margin of profit on the trading of essential commodities? Such com trol could remain in force until a steady balance were ensured and until the provinces had taken a concrete attitude on matters within their scope. I am deeply convinced that the government, whose policy it is to grant justice to all, will continue to ensure our country's economic stability.
The worker may have his troubles, but our farmer also has his problems. Certain parts of the country are not conversant with the specialized character of our agriculture. Farming in our part of the country is not industrialized1; we cannot determine the amount paid in wages, the cost of purchasing and repairing heavy and: essential implements, or the profiit resulting from the sale of a particular product, be it ten, twenty, thirty or even fifty thousand bushels of wheat. Agriculture is a family undertaking. From dawn to dusk every member of the family helps, to the limits of his ability with the plowing, with mixed farming, the sowing, the haymaking, the harvesting, the weeding, the care of livestock, the supplying of firewood, the repairing of tools and so forth.
When the holidays come around', the younger children take the herds to the pasture grounds, put hay in carts and do all sorts of chores to lighten the parents' burden. All efforts combined produce, at the end of the year, a modest income, which cannot be compared with that derived from the large farms of western Canada. Very often, the children, from the youngest to the eldest do not receive any salary. They live together, happy to join in the family's occupation. The father acts as a sort of trustee of his children's earnings. When they marry or leave the home, he gives each son his rightful share by purchasing a farm or shop or by handing over to him a modest sum of money.
In all fairness, the family of the workingman, the farmer or the small wage-earner should be provided with a sufficient budget to meet essential expenditure. Because the
price of various necessities has risen, I feel that present income tax levies are extremely burdensome on the head of the household when they compel him to deprive his dependents of what is essential to their health or intellectual advancement.
Has the time not yet come to grant full income tax exemption to married people earning no more than $2,500 without reducing, in any way, family allowance grants? Would it not be fitting to authorize deduction of the amounts required for classical or university training? In order to keep our youth in Canada and1 to foster new homes, I feel an exemption of at least $1,250 would be warranted. These are not maximum figures, of course, and our people would enthusiastically welcome more liberal exemptions.
Mr. Speaker, the income tax legislation, as interpreted and administered, is working a hardship on our fine people. The farmer is not allowed to deduct the wages which he has administered on behalf of his son, unless there was an actual handing over of the money during the year in which it was earned. This is likely to harm the unity which should prevail within the family, and to impair teamwork. I believe that the act should be amended so as to allow such wages as deductible expenses, when it is established that the money was earned by the son's work, even though it was administered by the head of the family.
In certain cases, the interpretation of the law varies with the district. For example, in some places, when a young farmer inherits from his father a farm which he might have earned by his own non-remunerated labour, a tax is levied just as if he were the recipient of an annual revenue. In other places, the amount is spread over several years, which might exempt the heir from the obligation of paying a tax. This seems right to me, since, in- the first instance, the estate is to a large extent mortgaged by succession duties and income tax. I therefore suggest that there be but one -interpretation of the law so that it may, in future, tend to ease the burden placed upon our farmers.
Let us not forget that it was the farmers of Quebec who opened up this country to civilization, cleared it and brought to confederation its greatest strength. Their traditions and the nature of their farming operations must be protected.
Mr. Speaker, at this critical moment in history, when our economy needs to be enlightened by science, it is of the utmost importance that farming in the east receive

The Address-Mr. J. A. Ross
particular attention. The western plains have opened for us the doors of foreign trade, but it is the mixed farming of the east which has always been the cornerstone of our internal economy.
Do I need to remind the house that Ste. Anne de la Poeatiere, in the historic county of Kamouraska, is an educational and agricultural centre unmatched in this country. It has the oldest agricultural college in Canada. Devoted priests and enlightened and experienced farmers have brought that institution into being by contributing their own -funds. As a result of the untiring work of those advocates of farming and their successors, Ste. Anne is today the beacon which sends forth its light throughout eastern Quebec and even as far as the maritimes. The college gives a first-rate classical education while the High School of Agriculture and Fisheries trains farmers and fishermen. Nearby, -the Dominion experimental farm makes available to farmers of the district the results of its research and experience. But the more farming develops, the more does it need the help of science. Practical research should be intensified.
Soil analysis, acclimatization of new varieties and the study of plant diseases should be carefully fostered in order to adapt Canadian agriculture to present needs. I therefore ask the Right Hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) to provide us with liberal grants for the advancement of agricultural science, which is so essential to our country's progress.
In truth, only a full measure of social justice will supply us with effective weapons against communism. The family is the basis upon which rests any well-organized Christian society. Union among our families, balanced relations among the various classes, and the economic liberation of the masses will help us pursue our glorious rise towards an era of progress and happiness. Man, happy to live freely of the fruit of his labour, will never accept communist or socialist slavery. Let us keep the farmer on the soil, the worker in the factory by helping them over passing difficulties.
As long as our farmers keep working with a smile, as long as they derive greater strength from their faith, as long as they remain the masters of their heritage, neither socialist nor communist materialism can stop in then-hearts the flow of Christian life. The clamour of war will never muffle the song of bells echoing with the joy and pain of the -tiller of the soil. At the end of a life filled with toil and sacrifice, dedicated to his family and to his country, his duty done and the promise
of eternal peace so soon to be fulfilled, he may say with Lamartine:

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to offer a few observations in the debate in reply to the governor general's speech of December 5, 1947, at the commencement of this session, and- I wish to refer especially to a portion of the speech which states:
My ministers are concerned with increases in prices which have added to the cost of living. In certain instances, increases were felt to have been unjustified and price ceilings have been restored. Officials in the departments of government most immediately concerned have been directed to keep under constant supervision conditions of production and supply which tend to raise the level of consumer prices.
The demand for the products of our primary industries generally continues to remain at high levels. In view of the price fixed for the 19481949 crop year under the wheat agreement with the United Kingdom, you will be asked to consider a measure to provide for an increase in the initial payment to producers.
A few days prior to our convening after the Christmas recess the Canadian Association of Consumers, under date of January 20, sent a brief to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), and, I think, to all hon. members, pointing out fhe difficulties of the consumers across this nation with respect to the advancing cost of living. In- one paragraph they point out specifically that the reimposition of subsidies on hard wheat and coarse grains to bring down the price to consumers of meat, bread and dairy products is necessary to halt the inflationary trend.
I wish, first of all, to endorse most heartily the remarks made this afternoon by my colleague the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks), and more especially the arguments he so well advanced on- behalf of our veterans and their dependents, many of whom find it very difficult to provide the essential food) for their families. The hon. member did a splendid job in indicating the difficulties of these citizens of Canada who have done so much for us.
I wish also to compliment my colleague the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) on the stand he took with reference to the assistance, which was announced prior to the Christmas adjournment, of ten per cent in some cases to our veterans and their dependents. As he so well pointed out, that is altogether inadequate. I add my word to those
The Address-Mr. J. A. Ross

we have heard from other members at this time on behalf of our veterans and- their dependents, who find it so difficult under these conditions to provide properly for themselves and their families. I hope the situation will be reconsidered in the near future.
I have here the Economic Annalist, a journal which is put out under the authority of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and his statistical branch. It is dated November, 1947, and at page 77 it refers to the Geneva conference of the food and agriculture organization of the united nations. The director general, Sir John Boyd Orr, addressing the conference, said:
The report placed before you today raises problems of the utmost gravity. There is the continuing world food shortage. In Europe next winter-
That is this winter.
-and spring, three years after the end of hostilities, there will be millions who will be worse fed than they were during the war.
You will hear arguments throughout the country about how well off the producers of these particular foods in Canada are today, that is to say, the farm producers. In the same journal there is a report on a survey which was conducted by the officials of the federal Department of Agriculture and the University of Manitoba in southwestern Manitoba, giving the actual experience of 216 farm operators as disclosed by farm business records obtained in the summer of 1946, which form the basis for the description of the economics of farm organization in southwestern Manitoba. I quote from the report:
The Information was obtained through a farm business survey conducted jointly by the economics division, marketing service, dominion Department of Agriculture and the department of political economy, University of Manitoba. A record of the entire farm business for the year June 1, 1945, to May 31, 1946, was obtained from each of these farmers.
The area for the study was the extreme southwestern portion of Manitoba lying mostly in Manitoba crop district one. This area took in Reston, Melita and Boissevain. Their type of farming was set forth in the report. As regards land utilization, the total area per farm averaged 547 acres at Reston, 529 acres at Melita and 471 acres at Boissevain. In the report there is a great deal of detail which I will not go into, but I should like to set forth some of the essential points given.
In livestock distribution, it is stated that all the farms studied had some livestock. Of the 216 farms, 211 raised cattle and 140 kept hogs. All but seven farmers had some horses used entirely or partly for farm power. Poultry

raised primarily to provide eggs, and meat for home consumption was found on most farms. Very few farmers raised many sheep.
In terms of animal units, the total per farm for all farms studied was 28-5 animal units. This was distributed as follows: cattle 18-5; horses 7-4; hogs 1-7; and other livestock, mainly poultry, 0-9. The largest number of farm animals was found on farms in the Melita district. These averaged 30 animal units per farm as compared with 29-5 animal units at Reston and 26-2 at Boissevain.
In the matter of farm capital, the average investment was $11,062 per farm for all farms studied. This was distributed as follows: real estate $5,122; livestock $2,264; machinery and equipment $2,858; feed, seed and supplies $818.
I think that is pretty much a self-contained type of farming among these 216 which were surveyed. As to the financial progress made, the report states:
While some of the farmers have been operating the present farm for a long -time, 67 per cent of the farmers have commenced operating the present farm within the last fifteen years. For all the farms studied, the average number of years the present farm has been operated by the present operator is 13' 1 years . . . The present over-all net worth is $13,895 per farmer, representing an average increase in net worth per farm of $713 per year as a result of income from all sources. When calculated on the basis of income from farm activities only, the average increase in net worth per farm was $600.
This was up to June 1, 1946. Production in 1947 had decreased considerably, as most people know. I do not think anyone will argue that these farmers have made any great killing during this time. I do not think it can be successfully contended that they have been wheat mining. They have pretty well established the self-contained farm and produced food, generally speaking, for others as well as for themselves.
I said I wished to deal with a few particular items set out in the report of the consumers' organization. I sympathize sincerely with these people. During the past recess when I was at home I visited a number of homes in Manitoba where there were small children, and in my opinion the net income received by the head of the average family could not provide sufficient milk, meat and other foods to take care of these children properly. Neither the children nor the other members of the family could be properly cared for on the income received.
That is the situation we find in Canada today. It is the situation in cities, towns and villages because the wages of the so-called white-collar class throughout the war years were unfairly frozen. The members of this

The Address-Mr. J. A. Ross
class have received no increase in income as labour has, and where there is a small family we find hardship and suffering. These people cannot properly provide the necessities of life, on the income they have.
The first item I wish to refer to is bread.
I do not know whether many people have yet realized in Canada that throughout the war years the farmer subsidized all the consumers of the country as well as the people of Britain, so far as bread is concerned, and they are still doing so. That is the situation today.
I am not sure where some of these difficulties arise. I know that in 1926, which was in normal times, in the city of Winnipeg when wheat was selling at $1.56% and flour at $9.25 a barrel, bread sold at seven cents a loaf. In . 1946, the first year following the war when the miller was buying wheat for 77% cents, bread was selling at eight cents a loaf. He was paying less for wheat and charging more for bread. I do not know what the exact figures are for bread today, but I believe the prices is ten or eleven cents in Winnipeg; and the miller still buys wheat for less than he paid in 1926, because he buys wheat from the producer in the prairie provinces on the basis of $1.55 Tort William, the same figure at which the wheat is supplied to the United Kingdom under the contract.
Obviously, therefore, there is a disparity that someone will have to explain. I cannot tell the house how it comes about, but these are the figures, and there is that added cost which is not in the wheat that is used in making the bread.
There is one matter which has often been discussed in the past, to which I will refer now, and it will be discussed in the future as well. That is this matter of wheat and the fact that the prairie producer has subsidized all the consumers in this nation, let me repeat, as well as the consumers of Great Britain. The Minister of Agriculture, with his prairie advisers, made the greatest speculation-some say gamble-in wheat the world has ever known. They sold short 600,000,000 bushels, 440.000,000 bushels of which had not then even been seeded, over a term of four years and at prices which no man could foresee. The world price of wheat, which the right hon. gentleman vainly tries to brush aside at every meeting on the prairies turned against these gentlemen.
On the last day of this session before we adjourned for Christmas, on December 19, the Minister of Agriculture stated that there is no such thing as a world price of wheat. He and his advisers have lost their gamble and so our farmers have to forfeit huge sums in cash
on this wheat they have produced. The Minister of Agriculture may argue with words, but he will find it difficult to argue against simple arithmetic or the terms that he himself placed in the United Kingdom-Canada wheat agreement. Why should the prairie farmers alone subsidize Britain and the Canadian people with cheap wheat? I am not arguing that they should not be subsidized; but, if so, that subsidy should be borne by all the taxpayers of this nation, as has so often been pointed out in this house. Every time we refer to the loss that has been borne by these producers, the figures have become greatly increased and are much more alarming. I have before me the Searle grain index report under date of January 21 of this year. Right at the beginning I want to say that no member on any side of this House of Commons has ever refuted any of the figures contained in that report which their able research men put out. These are authentic figures which can be proven if anyone has doubt about them. According to this report, under the heading of cash losses to farmers:
From August 1, 1946, to December 31, 1947, a period of seventeen months, the loss taken by our wheat growers on the wheat they have delivered to country elevators comes to the following staggering sums, all as compared with what farmers would have received had they enjoyed the full world price set daily by the Canadian wheat board itself for class 2 wheat.
The Minister of Agriculture to whom I referred is a member of the wheat committee and responsible for the wheat board and the setting of this price. The report continues:
(a)	On the wheat hauled by farmers and intended for shipment to Britain, $296 million.
(b)	On the wheat hauled by farmers and intended for domestic consumption in Canada, $152 million.
A grand total of $448 million lost by prairie farmers in seventeen months; a loss equal to more than the value of one whole prairie wheat crop; a loss equal to the entire dominion receipts from all forms of taxation in the year 1938; a loss which averages $1,900 for each prairie wheat-growing family, and with the losses still increasing greatly day by day.
It will be remembered, too, that prior to the start of the wheat agreement August 1, 1946, the government had marketed our f armers' wheat for several years at less than the world price. These losses to farmers for the years 1943, 1944 and 1945, come to an additional $409 million.
So, Mr. Speaker, there is a total loss since 1943 of $857 million on wheat produced by the prairie farmers of this country. That is a heavy subsidy to ask one class of people to carry for that term of years, especially when you remember that, on the other hand, they were the only class of people making such a contribution as that who were so controlled.

I am not going to argue about exports and subsidizing the consumers of this country. Nobody has objected to that. But all the other producers who have been exporting to the other markets of the world have been allowed by this government to receive the world prevailing prices. I have often mentioned the implement manufacturers, the lumber producers and so on, but the farmers have been the only class of people to be put in the strait-jacket by the government of the day. More than that, the policies of this government in this respect and in respect of the controls on the essentials of food1 that I have mentioned and am going to refer to, have been directly responsible for creating the chaos that we find ourselves in at the present day.
I made some reference to the Minister of Agriculture and what he pointed out on December 19. If anyone wishes to refer to the remarks themselves, he may do so by turning to page 504 of Hansard. There, speaking about wheat and the Chicago and Winnipeg markets, the right hon. gentleman stated:
I am saying that there has not been a world price during the last few years.
He made the same statement at Dauphin and many other places throughout the prairie provinces during the past few months. In this report which I have of the Canadian wheat board for the crop year 1945-1946, there is written in at page 10 a copy of the United Kingdom wheat contract, and a portion of it reads as follows:
In determining the actual price in the last two years regard will be had to the extent to which the agreed price for the first two years falls below the world price for that period. Our farmers are therefore protected from crippling losses should there be a world slump in wheat prices. This is the commercial advantage which Canada secures.
If there has been no world price, as the Minister of Agriculture has said, I should like him to explain what that "world price" in the sentence there meant at that particular time. The immediate ex-minister of trade and commerce gives full credit to the right lion, gentleman for having negotiated that agreement and for being responsible for the drafting of it. I think he owes some explanation to this -house if it does not mean anything and if there is not a. world price.
Before I leave that matter of wheat I -want to say-and I am speaking -personally now, and stating my own views on the matter- that the majority of the farmer-producers are at the present time dissatisfied with this marketing set-up and the -price they are receiving in Canada. A recent poll shows

that some sixty-five -per cent are dissatisfied with the present state of affairs respecting the marketing of their wheat. I fully realize that in my time we have had two royal commissions which studied and investigated the marketing of wheat in this country. I fully realize that last session we had before this house amendments to the Canadian Wheat Board Act, and that in spite of the request by the leader of this party, myself and others, the government refused -to refer those amendments to the standing committee on agriculture. Notwithstanding all that, I firmly believe-and I make it as a personal request- that -the government, before they bring in certain legislation on further payments, should grant a reference to this standing committee on agriculture and make that reference broad enough so that they can thoroughly investigate the production and marketing of this great commodity which is so essential to human welfare throughout the world. It is the greatest export commodity produced in this nation. As the Minister of Agriculture and others have said, it is the most essential food for human welfare in all the countries throughout this world. I would hope that the government could see their way clear to grant a reference to this standing committee on agriculture so that they could call before that committee the officials of the producing and marketing agencies-yes, and consumers if you like-of this nation of ours and that we should at least have an opportunity of trying to find out what is best with regard to this great commodity in the interests of these people at this time. I think we are entitled to that. I trust the government will give serious consideration to that suggestion, because to me wheat- is an important item in the economy of this country. At -present we have a government monopoly the like of which we have never had in all the history of this nation. Surely this committee should be entitled to investigate and study that very important matter.
I want to say something about dairy products. Previously I stated that I liad seen families in cities, towns and villages, who in my opinion were not able to provide sufficient milk for their youngsters. Today in many centres milk is costing more than- twice what it cost before the war. I am sure hon. members have all read of the trouble that has been experienced by the milk distributors in the great Winnipeg area. I have complimented these organizations on the job -they have done in keeping the producers from going out on strike, I want to point out to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the members of this

house that, according to 'the officials of that organization, some sixty dairy herds in that area have been liquidated and put completely out of production in the last few months. That is a serious matter. Even in the vicinity of my own trading centre of Melita-and I know the same is true of other sections of the west-many of the local dairy herds have gone out of production; and this town of Melita, with a population of some eight hundred, has to have milk shipped from Winnipeg and Brandon in order to supply the consumers. That is a situation which should not exist in an agricultural community; yet it is true in many centres throughout the prairie provinces. The price of milk varies in different centres, ranging anywhere from seventeen to twenty cents a quart today. Again I say that is a serious situation, and it has been brought about by the policies of this government throughout the war years and in the period that has intervened since the end of the war.
I have here a reference to Britain's subsidized farmers. A year ago I put a good deal on record in reference to their farm act, setting out how they could severely penalize a farmer for not carrying out their instructions. He can be sentenced to jail, as well as assessed a heavy fine. This reference deals with the matter from another angle, and gives the other side of the picture. According to this article the government of Britain are still spending a colossal sum of money to subsidize food. They are spending $1,600 million annually in food subsidies. That is a sizeable sum of money, which must be raised in taxes, and a great deal of it goes directly to the farmers in order to keep down the cost of food to the consumers. Milk, which sells to housewives for fifteen cents a quart, even in country areas, is heavily subsidized. That price is much lower than milk is costing us right in our farm areas. Over there, farmers get approximately eighty cents a dozen for eggs, a great deal more than the price we are
receiving for the eggs we sell to Britain. Those eggs are sold in grocery stores one at a time for about three and a half cents each, or at about half their cost, and the subsidy covers the balance.
I do not want to labour this matter, but I do want to point out that notwithstanding the fact that this colossal sum of money is being spent, the situation is very unsatisfactory in Britain todlay. The article I have before me states:
Meanwhile, life in Britain is becoming harder and harder for the bulk of the people. Only officials, bureaucrats and politicians are immune from the harrowing anxieties which all other classes of the community daily endure.
It goes on to point out that they must line up in queues and then in many cases, despite their ration tickets, they are not able to get the food they need for their families. It discusses the position of the butcher, who is not able to obtain the meat he requires; of the fishmonger, who does not know when he will be able to get enough fish; of the baker, the grocer, and so on. I do not want to weary the house further with this, but I do point out that the condition existing in Britain at present is very unsatisfactory.
I believe I have said enough in regard to wheat and milk to indicate that if this situation is allowed to continue it will not be long until we shall be unable to procure the necessities of life; and that should not be allowed to happen in this country. It is the result of very bad administration.
